--- title: "Conditional diffusion" lecture-number: 16 date: 2026-11-20 resources: - pics/lec16/demos.js - pics/lec16/demos-data.js --- ## Tuesday's lab :::{.incremental} * A tiny UNet, trained for a few minutes to predict the clean digit, gave smudgy blobs that only sometimes looked like digits. * A `UNet2DModel` with attention, trained with the same data, epochs and loss, did noticeably better. * With the DDPM scheduler, the digit was gone well before halfway through the 1,000 steps. Why? ::: ## Small images disappear sooner The same schedule, the same noise level, two sizes of the same photo: ![](pics/lec16/forward-res.jpg){width="62%"} ::: {.note-text} $t = 0, 100, 200, 300$. Top: 256 × 256 pixels. Bottom: 32 × 32, the size of the lab's digits. Photo: scikit-image sample data, CC0. ::: :::{.incremental} * At 256 × 256, each feature covers many pixels, so the eye can average the noise away. At 32 × 32 there's much less to average over. * So a schedule that suits large images wastes many of its steps on small ones. ::: ## The cosine schedule, revisited How much of the image is left, $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$, for the lab's linear schedule and for the cosine schedule: ```{=html} ``` . . . With the linear schedule, less than 10% of the image is left by $t = 644$. With the cosine schedule, that happens only at $t = 935$. ## Try it: schedule and size ```{=html}
256 × 256
32 × 32
t = 300
``` Image left: $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t} =$ [0.56]{.l16-sig .l16-num}, the same for both sizes. Only how much you can still *see* differs. ::: aside Drag the slider or the chart, and switch schedule. Each size has its own fixed noise. ::: # Adding control ## Which image? Last lecture's model generates *an* image: whatever comes out of the noise it started from. :::{.incremental} * In probability terms, it learned to sample from $p(x)$, the distribution of training images. * Usually we want to say *which* image: a 7, a sneaker, "an astronaut riding a horse". We want to sample from $p(x \mid y)$, where $y$ is the **condition**. * This is **conditional generation**. Today the condition is a class label. Next time it's a text prompt. ::: ## Try it: choosing the shape :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="52%"} ```{=html}
the data, coloured by label
``` ::: ::: {.column width="48%"} ::::: {.small-text} Back to two-number "images". Now each point has a label: ring, line or blobs. ```{=html}
Add noise:
Generate 300 points, in 100 steps:
``` "Any shape" uses the best guess over all the points: $p(x)$. A label restricts the best guess to that shape's points: $p(x \mid y)$. ::::: ::: :::: ## The idea Give the network $y$ as one more input, during training *and* during sampling. $$\hat\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) \quad\longrightarrow\quad \hat\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, y)$$ :::{.incremental} * In training, $y$ is the label of the image that was noised. The network can use it to predict the noise better: knowing "this is a 7" helps to tell stroke from noise. * In sampling, we choose $y$ ourselves, and keep it fixed for every step. Each step then nudges the image towards a 7. ::: . . . But how do we feed a label into a UNet? The same way we already feed it $t$. # How the network hears $t$ ## A timestep embedding $t$ is a single integer, from 0 to 999. The network needs a vector. :::{.incremental} * First, sines and cosines of $t$ at a range of frequencies. This is exactly the **sinusoidal positional encoding** from the transformer, with the step $t$ in place of the token's position. * Then a small two-layer network (an MLP), so the model can learn what to make of it. * In the `UNet2DModel` you'll use in the lab, that's 32 sines and cosines, turned into a **time embedding** of 128 numbers. ::: ## Try it: what the network is told about $t$ ```{=html}
t = 250
``` ::: {.smaller-text} Top: the 32 numbers for step $t$, before the MLP (orange $+1$, grey $-1$). Below: the same for every step, one thin column each. Every step gets its own pattern, just as every token position does: the slow numbers say roughly when, the fast ones pin down exactly when. ::: ## Where it goes ```{=html} ``` :::{.incremental} * Each convolutional (ResNet) block in the UNet has its own linear layer, which maps the embedding to one number per channel of its feature map. * That number is added to every pixel of the channel: a bias that depends on $t$. So every block, at every resolution, knows how noisy its input is. ::: # Adding a class ## A class embedding is a lookup table A label is one of a fixed set of classes, just like a token is one of a fixed vocabulary. So we embed it the same way: one learned vector per class. ::: {#0af8e8d8 .cell output-location='fragment' execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import torch class_embedding = torch.nn.Embedding(10, 128) # 10 classes, 128 numbers each time_embedding = torch.randn(1, 128) # stands in for the real one y = torch.tensor([7]) embedding = time_embedding + class_embedding(y) # just add them embedding.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` torch.Size([1, 128]) ``` ::: ::: . . . The rows start random and are learned with everything else. Nothing tells the model what "7" means: it finds out from which images carry that label. ## In `diffusers` ```python model = UNet2DModel( sample_size=32, in_channels=1, out_channels=1, block_out_channels=(32, 64, 128, 256), num_class_embeds=10, # adds a 10 × 128 class embedding table ) noise_pred = model(noisy_images, t, class_labels=labels).sample ``` :::{.incremental} * The class embedding is added to the time embedding, and the sum reaches every block by the route we just saw. The rest of the network is unchanged. * This model has 15,892,033 parameters. The class table is 1,280 of them, under 0.01%. ::: ## What changes in training ```python for batch in dataloader: clean_images, labels = batch["images"], batch["labels"] # labels: new noise = torch.randn_like(clean_images) t = torch.randint(0, 1000, (len(clean_images),)) noisy_images = scheduler.add_noise(clean_images, noise, t) noise_pred = model(noisy_images, t, class_labels=labels).sample # new loss = F.mse_loss(noise_pred, noise) ... ``` :::{.incremental} * The noising process, the schedule and the loss are exactly as before. * The labels are the only new data, and many datasets already have them. ::: ## What changes in sampling ```python x = torch.randn(8, 1, 32, 32) labels = torch.full((8,), 7) # "eight 7s, please" for t in scheduler.timesteps: noise_pred = model(x, t, class_labels=labels).sample x = scheduler.step(noise_pred, t, x).prev_sample ``` . . . One label for the whole trajectory, every step. That's all. # Does it work? ## Same noise, different label A small class-conditional model (1.5M parameters, no attention), trained on MNIST for about 20 minutes on a laptop. In each row, all ten images share the same noise, from start to finish; each column asks for a different digit. ![](pics/lec16/same-noise.png){width="100%"} . . . The label decides *which* digit. The noise has a say in *how* it's drawn: compare the slant in the first row with the second. And not every request succeeds: look at the 5 in the last row. ## Same label, different noise Eight 7s, from eight different starting noises: ![](pics/lec16/sevens.png){width="80%"} . . . The model has learned a distribution of 7s, not a single 7. Not all of them are good: one is a blob, and one could pass for a 2. Twenty minutes isn't much training. ## Between two classes A class embedding is just a vector, so we can hand the model one it never saw in training: a blend of the rows for 1 and 7. ![](pics/lec16/blend.png){width="45%"} ::: aside From left to right, 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% of the way from 1 to 7, all from the same starting noise. ::: ## Try it: label and noise ```{=html}
the image \(x_t\)
the model's guess \(\hat x_0\)
Ask for:
Ask for:
or blend 1 → 7: 100% of the way to 7
Starting noise:
finished
``` ::: aside Bottom row: the finished image for each label, from the same starting noise and the same fresh noise at every step. Only the label differs. Click one to look at it. ::: ## Limitations :::{.incremental} * **Only the classes it was trained on.** A new class means new training data and retraining. Compare CLIP's zero-shot classifier, which just needed a new prompt. * **Similar classes get confused**, especially with a short training run. In the lab you'll find out which ones. * **The label can be under-used.** At small $t$, the image already shows what it is, so the label adds little. The network can reduce its loss a lot while largely ignoring $y$. ::: . . . Next lecture: conditioning on text instead of a label, and a trick to make the model pay *more* attention to the condition. ## Summary :::{.incremental} * A **conditional** model samples from $p(x \mid y)$: we choose $y$, and every denoising step takes it into account. * The timestep reaches the UNet as an **embedding**: sines and cosines, then an MLP, then added as a per-channel bias in every block. * A class label becomes an embedding from a **lookup table**, and is simply added to the time embedding. * The data, the noise, the schedule and the loss are unchanged. Only the conditioning signal is new. * Every later kind of conditioning, text included, is a variation on this idea: turn the condition into vectors, and give them to every block. :::
